newsitem.title: USA: FBI workers cheer agent disciplined over Jewell.
newsitem.headline: FBI workers cheer agent disciplined over Jewell.

text.p: A veteran FBI agent disciplined for his conduct in last year's investigation of former Olympic bomb suspect Richard Jewell was cheered by dozens of colleagues Thursday as he returned to work after a five-day suspension.

More than 100 FBI employees lined the sidewalk leading to the entrance to the bureau's Atlanta office to show support for Don Johnson, a rank-and-file agent who they say has been made a scapegoat by embarrassed FBI brass in Washington.

Johnson held his head high and walked slowly past his cheering co-workers at 7:45 a.m. outside the FBI's suburban office building, but he said nothing to the television cameras that showed up to record the event.

An agent with more than 20 years of experience, he was suspended without pay over an interview with Jewell that took place last July, on the day the former Olympic security guard became the only named suspect in the bomb investigation.

The bombing, which remains unsolved, left two people dead and more than 100 wounded at Centennial Olympic Park last July, during the height of the Atlanta Games. Jewell's lawyers contend that Johnson and other agents tried to trick their client into waiving his rights by telling him their interrogation was part of a training video.

Jewell was cleared of suspicion last November after being hounded by the FBI and the news media for nearly three months. Johnson was later disciplined along with David Tubbs and Woody Johnson, special-agents-in-charge who were reprimanded.

FBI agents who turned out to greet Johnson said they believed responsibility for the case rested with FBI Director Louis Freeh. "He (Johnson) was only doing exactly what he was told," agent Harry Grogan told reporters.
Lin Wood, an attorney for Jewell, who plans to sue FBI officials, said he too believes Johnson and his colleagues had been used as scapegoats.

"I believe these agents were acting on orders. I think they have been made scapegoats. And I think the punishment they have received was intentionally light so they would, in effect, 'take one' for the bureau," said Wood, who believes the agents should be fired if they acted alone.

He also charged the FBI was dragging its feet on an internal investigatio,n which had yet to produce a full report. "This agency is going to stonewall, it's going to whitewash, it's going to cover up to protect itself and its agents and, I believe, its director," Wood said.

At a weekly Justice Department press briefing in Washington, Acting Deputy Attorney General Seth Waxman had no comment on Johnson's return to work, saying disciplinary measures stemming from the case were pending under appeal.
But Johnson's supporters said the agent was mulling an appeal of his suspension and suggested he might at some point consider speaking publicly about his treatment.
